strengths: Originality/significance: The paper introduces a useful inference-time notion of “token sample complexity” and connects finite-context self-attention to its measure-valued infinite-token formulation. Studying how convergence depends on attention geometry and token anisotropy is timely and potentially valuable for long-context models.

Soundness: The uniform-convergence analysis in Theorem 4.2 is technically ambitious. The manuscript provides substantial appendices, explicit parameter dependence, proof sketches, and extensions to moments, covariance, Gaussian inputs, and multi-head attention.
The hardmax calculation offers an interesting qualitative insight: extreme-value behavior can produce logarithmically slow convergence rather than an ordinary polynomial rate.

Presentation: The main narrative is generally clear, the distinction from conventional training-sample complexity is well motivated, and the synthetic and real-data plots communicate the proposed slowdown mechanism effectively.

Limitations and ethics: The authors appropriately acknowledge that tightness of the general upper bound remains open and that rates depend strongly on the token distribution. The work presents no evident material ethical risk.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central finite-sample high-probability claim in Theorem 5.3 is not established by its proof. The sampling term J is bounded by invoking the CLT and a chi-squared quantile, but a CLT supplies an asymptotic distribution, not the asserted non-asymptotic probability bound for every n satisfying the theorem’s stated condition. No Berry–Esseen remainder or applicable concentration inequality is given. Since Theorem 5.3 is advertised as the main contribution, this is a material gap rather than a minor omission.

The same proof contains incorrect moment algebra: for a sub-Gaussian parameter matrix Σ it writes E||X||² = ||Σ||₂, whereas generally E||X||² = tr(Cov(X)) ≤ tr(Σ), not the spectral norm. Related dimension and notation inconsistencies occur because attention outputs lie in R^k while h is declared on R^d, and A is defined both with and without the 1/sqrt(k) scaling. These issues make the exact theorem statements and constants unreliable.

The empirical study does not adequately validate the theory’s setting. The analysis concerns dense, permutation-equivariant softmax attention over i.i.d. tokens without positional information, whereas the real-data experiments use sparse BigBird attention, positional interpolation, ordered and dependent text, and a multi-layer network. Sparse neighborhoods and positions fundamentally change which tokens participate in each normalization. Merely observing a correlation between fitted slopes and a proposed horizon does not show that the theorem explains that behavior.

The real-data power-law exponents are fitted over only n=1000–3000, a threefold range, against a finite reference of 500,000 tokens. The manuscript does not report sensitivity to the fitting interval, finite-reference bias, alternative functional forms, or uncertainty in the fitted exponents/correlation. Thus claims that experiments “confirm” the predictions or demonstrate a power-law regime are too strong.

The synthetic evidence compares empirical slopes with an upper-bound exponent but supplies no lower bound establishing tightness. Important simulation details—including the n grid/range, number of trials, construction and scaling of A, optimizer/regression choices, and uncertainty for fitted slopes—are absent from the paper. A statement that code is in supplementary material is not enough to make the reported agreement independently assessable.

The hardmax result is narrower than the surrounding interpretation suggests. At A=∞ the population Gaussian softmax operator itself is not a well-defined finite attention limit; Proposition 5.5 instead studies cancellation in the empirical average under one-dimensional symmetry. This does not establish convergence of the attention map or transformed distribution in the same sense as the preceding results.

Presentation/reproducibility: Several theorem conditions are inconsistent or malformed—for example, Corollaries C.4/C.6 use n ≥ 4(1−1/δ)n^(1/8), whose right-hand side is negative for δ in (0,1), unlike Theorem 5.3’s 1/δ−1. The undefined polynomial factors also obscure meaningful finite-sample requirements. These errors, together with the missing experimental specification, prevent others from reliably building on the main claims without substantial revision.

strengths: The measure-based framing of inference-time "token sample complexity" is potentially useful. Separating uniform convergence of the attention map from convergence of aggregate output statistics is conceptually sensible and reasonably original, particularly for dependent self-attention queries, keys, and values.

The paper is technically ambitious: it attempts explicit dependence on token anisotropy and attention geometry, includes extensive appendices, and analyzes an exactly tractable one-dimensional Gaussian hardmax limit.
The empirical section covers synthetic data and several languages, datasets, layers, and moments, with 500 Monte Carlo repetitions. The main narrative and figures are generally readable.

The authors appropriately acknowledge that tightness of the sub-Gaussian bound remains open and that the i.i.d. assumption does not describe real token sequences. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: Theorem 5.3 is presented as a finite-sample, high-probability result, but its proof bounds the sampling term using an asymptotic CLT and delta method, asserting the confidence inequality only "for n large enough." No Berry-Esseen-type bound or explicit threshold connects this argument to the theorem's stated sample-size condition. Thus the advertised finite-sample guarantee is not established.

Soundness: The same proof incorrectly identifies E||X||^2 with ||Sigma||_2. Even for a Gaussian, E||X||^2 = tr(Sigma), not its spectral norm. Consequently, the claimed covariance bound and its dimension dependence are wrong as written. There are also inconsistent normalizations of the empirical processes in the Dudley arguments and inconsistent inclusion of the value matrix V, making the main derivations difficult to validate.

The central theoretical conclusion is overstated. An upper bound O(n^{-beta}) with beta < 1/2 does not demonstrate that convergence is genuinely slower than n^{-1/2}; a root-n process also satisfies such a weaker upper bound. Except for the singular A = infinity hardmax limit, the paper supplies no matching lower bounds. Calling the general rates "sharp in practice" or saying that the theory establishes a slowdown is therefore unsupported.

The hardmax theorem takes A = infinity before n tends to infinity. The paper does not control the approximation between finite-temperature softmax and hardmax uniformly in n, so this logarithmic result does not justify claims about ordinary Transformers with merely large matrix norms.

The real-data evaluation is poorly aligned with the theory. The analysis assumes dense, permutation-equivariant attention without positional information and i.i.d. tokens from a fixed distribution, whereas the experiments use sparse BigBird attention, positional interpolation, contextual and strongly dependent representations, and subsampling from one long sequence. The paper does not define a correspondence that makes these measured errors instances of the theoretical model.

The empirical evidence is too weak for the strong validation claims. Power laws are fitted only over n = 1000 to 3000, a factor-three range; the infinite-context target is replaced by a finite 500,000-token reference; and the cross-configuration horizon correlation is confounded by layer, language, and representation changes. Uncertainties for fitted exponents, controlled anisotropy ablations on real data, and comparisons against alternative predictors are absent. Figure 2 provides qualitative rather than convincing quantitative agreement with the claimed exponent.

Significance is limited by the modeling gap: increasing an i.i.d. empirical sample is not generally equivalent to extending a coherent language-model context, whose content distribution, positional structure, and hidden states change with length. No downstream task or end-to-end Transformer consequence is demonstrated.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript despite the claim that code is supplied: the seven exact text datasets/configurations, subsample-size grid, positional-interpolation implementation, multihead definition of the reported horizon, attention sparsity treatment after subsampling, and slope-fitting protocol are insufficiently specified. strengths: The paper introduces a useful inference-time notion of token sample complexity and clearly distinguishes it from training-sample complexity. The measure-valued formulation of attention is natural and potentially valuable for understanding long contexts.

The uniform convergence analysis uses appropriate empirical-process machinery and makes the dependence on attention geometry, token anisotropy, dimension, and radius explicit. Extending the analysis from compact support to sub-Gaussian distributions is technically meaningful.

Moment-level convergence and the one-dimensional Gaussian hardmax calculation are interesting additions beyond closely related mean-field analyses. The latter provides intuitive evidence that extreme-value selection can produce logarithmically slow behavior.

The experiments span synthetic Gaussian inputs, multiple languages and domains, all 12 BigBird layers, and both mean and covariance errors. Reporting repeated-sampling error bars and openly acknowledging that Gaussian-bound tightness remains unproved are positives.

The manuscript is generally well organized and readable, with substantial proofs in the appendix and no material research-ethics concerns. weaknesses: The central interpretation is stronger than the theory supports. Theorem 5.3 gives a loose upper bound O(n^{-beta}) with beta<1/2; such a bound is also satisfied by an actual n^{-1/2} rate and therefore does not establish that convergence is genuinely sub-parametric. The paper nevertheless repeatedly says that the theorem derives or explains slow convergence and calls the bound sharp, while the conclusion concedes that tightness is open.

The proof of Theorem 5.3 contains material gaps. It invokes a CLT to assert a finite-n, probability-at-least-1-delta inequality for the sampling term without a non-asymptotic argument. It also states E||X||^2=||Sigma||_2, whereas the relevant quantity is tr(Cov(X)) and is bounded by tr(Sigma), not generally by the spectral norm. Several steps omit the value-map factor ||V||, and the use of Lipschitzness to bound ||h(f(x))|| implicitly requires h(0)=0 or an explicit recentering argument.

The theorem statement hides essential dependence inside an unspecified polynomial P(sqrt(log n),L0). Its coefficients and degree may depend on A, V, Sigma, dimension, and delta, but this is not stated explicitly. Consequently, the result does not presently provide a reproducible token sample-complexity estimate for a desired error tolerance.

The hardmax second-moment argument is incomplete as written: uniform integrability of |Z_n| and |Y_n| only establishes first-moment convergence, whereas the claimed second-moment asymptotic requires uniform integrability of their squares. Exponential-tail arguments may repair this, but they are not supplied. There are also normalization and notation inconsistencies throughout the proofs, including treating multiplication by V as equality with multiplication by ||V||.

The real-data experiment is not a faithful validation of the stated model. The theory concerns dense, permutation-equivariant self-attention on i.i.d. tokens, whereas the experiment uses sparse BigBird attention, positional interpolation, contextual and ordered tokens, and highly dependent representations. The paper briefly notes only the i.i.d. mismatch and does not analyze how sparse masks or positional information alter the limiting operator.

The empirical evidence is too limited to substantiate a power-law convergence claim: real-data slopes are fitted over only n=1000 to 3000, a factor-three interval, against a finite Nmax reference rather than the population limit. The reported horizon correlation is moderate, and no alternative-rate fits, sensitivity to the fitting range, uncertainty on fitted exponents, or control for layer/dataset confounding is provided.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the claimed supplementary code. The manuscript does not precisely identify all seven datasets, the checkpoint and preprocessing choices, construction of the 500,000-token sequences, positional-interpolation details, synthetic matrices and sample-size grid, or the exact regression procedure. Presentation also suffers from inconsistent theorem/corollary references and a generic impact statement; limitations acknowledge non-tightness but not the substantial theory-to-experiment mismatch. Overall, the idea is promising, but the proof and evidential issues require substantial revision before the conclusions can be relied upon.

strengths: Original and potentially useful framing: “token sample complexity” cleanly separates inference-time context-length convergence from classical training-sample complexity.
The attention horizon H provides an interpretable connection between token geometry and attention parameters. The Gaussian hardmax analysis via extreme-value theory is particularly interesting.
The paper attempts an unusually broad validation, covering synthetic Gaussian data, BigBird and BERT representations, structured sampling, multiple languages/domains, and downstream classification.
The exposition is generally clear, with useful proof sketches, extensive appendices, readable figures, and an honest acknowledgement that tightness outside the hardmax setting remains open.
The work raises no material ethical concerns; experiments use established models and standard text datasets.
weaknesses: The central Theorem 5.3 is not soundly established as a finite-sample high-probability result. In Appendix C.6, the sampling term J is bounded by “applying the CLT” and a chi-square quantile. A CLT gives an asymptotic distribution, not the stated non-asymptotic probability inequality, and no Berry–Esseen or concentration argument is supplied.

The same proof contains consequential norm errors. It writes E||X||²=||Σ||₂ rather than tr(Σ) or an appropriate proxy bound. More seriously, Proposition C.14 bounds max_i||x_i|| using σ_B=||Σ^{1/2}B^T||₂, which controls ||Bx_i||, not ||x_i||; a dependence on B^{-1} is missing. It also uses ||f_n(x)||≤max_i||x_i|| despite the value map V, for which a factor ||V|| is generally required. These errors affect the optimized horizon-dependent bound rather than merely presentation.

Σ is defined as a non-unique sub-Gaussian proxy matrix, but it is subsequently described as the covariance and replaced by empirical covariance in the real-data experiments. General non-Gaussian distributions need not satisfy the stated MGF inequality with their covariance, so the theoretical status of the reported real-data horizons is not justified.

The claimed quantitative empirical match is overstated. The main theorem predicts β=1/[2(1+32H²)], while the Gaussian experiment compares against a different β=1/[2(1+H²)]. For real-data horizons around 40–600, either theoretical exponent is far smaller than the observed roughly 0.25–0.5 rates. The real experiments therefore show only a moderate negative correlation, not validation of the predicted rates.

Power-law exponents for the main representation experiments are fitted over only n=1000–3000, a factor-three range. There are no uncertainty intervals for fitted slopes or correlation coefficients, and layer/dataset effects may confound the relationship with H. The downstream study uses only five Monte Carlo repetitions.

The theory assumes i.i.d. tokens from a position-free marginal distribution, whereas real sequences contain strong dependence, positional encodings, and query-key structure. Randomly resampling token embeddings makes the theorem applicable to an artificial distribution, but does not by itself justify claims about increasing natural context length. Window experiments are useful evidence but remain qualitative and lack corresponding theory.

Reproducibility is inadequate: no code or artifact is identified, and important details are missing, including exact dataset subsets and preprocessing, random seeds, attention-head aggregation for H, construction of the 500k-token reference, positional-interpolation settings, regression procedure, and several fine-tuning and sampled-inference hyperparameters.

The manuscript is polished but contains unresolved inconsistencies and imprecisions, including dimension mismatches for h, a self-referential sample-size condition, unspecified polynomial constants in the main bound, and use of Θ in the proof where only upper bounds were derived. Given the flaws in the central convergence theorem and the limited quantitative support for its practical claims, substantial correction and reevaluation are required before acceptance.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper introduces a useful inference-time perspective on attention approximation and identifies a potentially informative interaction quantity, the attention horizon. The exact one-dimensional Gaussian hardmax calculation is an interesting contribution.

Soundness: The uniform-convergence analysis in Theorem 4.2 uses appropriate empirical-process ideas, and the extensive appendix makes a serious attempt to expose the technical argument rather than hiding it behind informal claims.

Evaluation: The authors examine synthetic Gaussian data, two pretrained model families, multiple languages/domains, structured sampling, and a downstream classification task. These experiments consistently reveal diminishing returns from additional sampled keys.

Presentation and ethics: The main narrative is generally clear, figures are legible, limitations such as the i.i.d. assumption and unknown tightness are acknowledged, and the work presents no evident material ethical risk.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim is not supported quantitatively by the stated theory. Theorem 5.3 gives only an upper bound with exponent 1/[2(1+32H^2)] and an unspecified polynomial prefactor, not an identified convergence rate. For the real-data examples H=19, 62, and 128, this exponent is orders of magnitude smaller than the observed exponents 0.47, 0.42, and 0.31. The experiments establish at most a moderate negative correlation with H (reported R around -0.6), not that the theoretical bound predicts or matches the rates.

There are material gaps or errors in the proof of the main moment result. In Appendix C.6, a CLT is used to assert a finite-n high-probability bound without a Berry-Esseen-type error or a distribution-dependent threshold. The proof also writes E||X||^2=||Sigma||_2, whereas only a trace-type bound follows. Proposition C.14 bounds max_i||x_i|| using a scale parameter for Bx_i, which is invalid for general B, and treats f_n as a convex combination of x_i despite the value map V. Consequently, Theorem 5.3 is not established as stated.

The paper conflates the sub-Gaussian parameter matrix Sigma with the covariance matrix. Definition 4.1 only assumes an MGF upper-bound parameter, yet Remark 5.2 calls it the covariance and the real-data experiments appear to estimate H using empirical covariance. For non-Gaussian embeddings, covariance need not be a valid sub-Gaussian proxy, so the empirical horizon may not be the quantity occurring in the theorem.

The Gaussian exponent is also presented too strongly. The manuscript calls the upper-bound curve a theoretical prediction and claims tight agreement, while Proposition D.23 supplies only an O bound. Appendix C.6 obtains a Theta expression for the optimized upper-bound function, not a matching lower bound on the actual error. The conclusion itself concedes that tightness remains open.

The practical significance is limited by a mismatch between the model and real long-context attention. The theory assumes exchangeable i.i.d. tokens, no positional information, and a single attention operator with fixed parameters. The main experiments create i.i.d. samples from a pooled set of contextual embeddings, thereby discarding order and dependence. The window experiment is empirical only, and the brief deep-composition corollary assumes fresh i.i.d. subsampling and bounded intermediate distributions. Thus the results do not justify broad claims about increasing the length of coherent Transformer contexts.

The empirical protocol is insufficiently controlled for the claimed mechanism. Rates are often fitted over only n=1000 to 3000, a factor-three range; uncertainty for fitted slopes and sensitivity to the fitting interval are not reported. Layer and dataset are substantial confounders in the horizon correlations. The downstream horizon stratification is not defined precisely, and K=5 repetitions is weak support for fitted power laws.

Reproducibility is inadequate in the manuscript: it omits exact dataset subsets, token construction, sampling details, random seeds, positional-interpolation implementation, rate-fitting procedure, most fine-tuning hyperparameters, and a code or configuration reference. These omissions are particularly important because the experiments involve approximately 500,000-token reference sets and nonstandard modification of BigBird attention.

Presentation contains additional imprecision, including inconsistent dimensions for h and f, ambiguous use of expectations over empirical measures, an implicit sample-size condition containing n on both sides, and references to results under inconsistent numbering. These issues make the main theorem difficult to interpret reliably.

strengths: Originality: The paper introduces a useful inference-time notion of token sample complexity and identifies the attention horizon H=||Σ^{1/2}AΣ^{1/2}|| as an interpretable coupling between token geometry and attention weights. This provides a fresh perspective beyond existing mean-field analyses.

Significance: Understanding diminishing returns from longer contexts and sampled-key attention is timely. The connection to downstream classification, where 25% of keys recovers most dense-model accuracy, suggests practical relevance.

Soundness strengths: The paper develops several complementary results: uniform convergence on bounded query sets, moment convergence for sub-Gaussian inputs, an exact logarithmic hardmax asymptotic in a one-dimensional Gaussian setting, and a heavy-tailed counterexample. The proofs contain substantial empirical-process and extreme-value analysis.

Evaluation: Experiments span controlled Gaussian data, a non-Gaussian synthetic distribution, BigBird, BERT, multiple languages/domains, structured window sampling, and an end-to-end classification task. The recurring negative association between horizon and fitted convergence rate is encouraging.

Presentation and ethics: The main ideas, theorem hierarchy, and proof sketches are generally clear, and the manuscript explicitly acknowledges that tightness outside the hardmax case remains open. The work raises no apparent material ethical concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness: The proof of Theorem 5.3 treats a central-limit-theorem approximation as a finite-sample high-probability inequality for the sampling term J, using a chi-squared quantile for a general non-Gaussian random vector. A CLT alone does not justify the stated probability bound. A Chebyshev-type argument may recover an O(n^{-1/2}) rate, but the theorem is not proved as written.

Soundness: Proposition C.14 bounds max_i||x_i|| using σ_B=||Σ^{1/2}B^T||, which controls ||Bx_i|| rather than ||x_i||. For arbitrary invertible B, a factor involving ||B^{-1}|| is required. The proof also omits the value map V when asserting that f_n(x) is a convex combination of the tokens. These errors affect the main tail argument, although they may be repairable at the level of prefactors.

Soundness and interpretation: Σ is defined only as a sub-Gaussian parameter matrix, but is repeatedly treated as the covariance. Such a parameter is non-unique, and a general sub-Gaussian vector need not be sub-Gaussian with its covariance matrix as the parameter. Consequently, the claimed intrinsic interpretation of H and the use of empirical covariance to connect the theorem to real-data experiments require additional assumptions or justification.

Claims of tightness are overstated. The main argument derives upper bounds but writes Θ at the end of the proof, and Proposition D.23 is likewise only an O bound. Empirical agreement for Gaussian simulations does not establish tightness. For real models, observed exponents around 0.25–0.5 are not quantitatively compared with the extremely small exponent 1/[2(1+32H²)] predicted at the reported large horizons; the evidence mainly supports a correlation, not the claimed quantitative token requirement.

Evaluation is less decisive than it first appears: real-data slopes are fitted over only n=1000–3000, a factor-of-three range, and horizon-rate correlations are moderate and visibly scattered. The manuscript does not clearly specify how horizons are aggregated across heads, how positional information and layerwise token dependence are handled, or enough details of the sampled-key intervention to rule out confounding by layer, dataset, or attention magnitude.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the scale of the empirical claims. No code or artifact link is provided, and important details such as seeds, preprocessing, exact text construction, fitting procedure and uncertainty for exponents, fine-tuning hyperparameters, per-head horizon computation, and reference-limit error are missing. The generic impact statement is acceptable for this theoretical work, but it does not discuss the computational cost of the large Monte Carlo experiments.
